The precision of our predictions for the lifetime of the B^0_s meson has been matched 
or surpassed by a previous calculation, and our method to enhance sensitivity 
via the $B^0_s\to J/\psi\phi$ decay has been confirmed. Utilizing 24.5 $ \rm fb^{-1} 
$ of LHCb data at 7 and 8 TeV, we have updated the measurement of the $ \rm 
MS$ lifetime to 1.479 $ \pm 0.006 \pm 0.005 $ ps. A similar measurement of the 
$ \rm MS$ lifetime for the B^0 meson has been achieved, with a result of 0.736 $ \pm 
0.007 \pm 0.001 $ ps based on 9 $ \rm fb^{-1} $ of LHCb data at 7, 8, and 13 
TeV. Both measurements are in line with previous findings and reinforce the 
constraints on theories beyond the Standard Model that could influence the weak 
dynamics of charmed quarks.

This study formulates a stochastic reflection principle for a class of stochastic control problems involving path-dependent reflection in a rough environment. The development of a suitable weak convergence result for a family of solutions, tailored to inputs with rapidly decreasing averages, enabled the creation of the reflection principle. The technique employed initially uses the Euler scheme to illustrate the concept, and then an alternative method based on an earlier result by Pedevenu is also presented. The associated numerical approximation and the convergence of the corresponding discretization schemes are discussed in the final section.

The direction of highest particle density in cosmic rays with energies above 4 EeV was studied using a 9.5 square kilometer array at the Pierre Auger Observatory. A method called Fourier analysis was used to identify the pattern of anisotropy in the sky. Initially detected anisotropy was found to be aligned with the dipole direction, and as the energy range was narrowed to 4-7.5 EeV, a shift in the anisotropy pattern became apparent. A study of the anisotropy amplitude with energy revealed a rise that is consistent with multiple sources of anisotropy, likely originating from the local and extragalactic components. The findings are in line with previous observations of the energy dependence of anisotropy, displaying a square root relationship with energy in the same energy range. The dipole anisotropy pattern was also examined in different azimuthal angles, revealing that the orientation of the largest particle density in the sky changes with energy, and may indicate the presence of a significant contribution from the extragalactic component of cosmic rays.

This research paper classifies all finite-dimensional Zinbiel algebras over a field that is algebraically closed, possessing a characteristic of either 0 or greater than 3. We find that these Zinbiel algebras are either two-dimensional nilpotent algebras, three-dimensional solvable algebras, or three-dimensional Lorentzian algebras. A detailed examination of these structures is provided, along with a discussion of their properties and parametric equations.

This research focuses on a new approach to identify the characteristics of the quark-gluon plasma in heavy-ion collisions by examining flow fluctuations. Our analysis introduces a new four-particle correlation observables, known as the six-point cumulant elliptic harmonic coefficient, which allows us to quantify the quark-gluon plasma's properties by analyzing six-particle distributions from heavy-ion collisions. We then develop a simulation-based method to determine this cumulant's relationship to the quark-gluon plasma's properties by using event generators that incorporate initial conditions, hydrodynamic simulations of the quark-gluon plasma, and jet propagation through the resulting medium. By analyzing six-particle distributions from 200 GeV Au+Au collisions from the STAR experiment, we find that their predicted patterns of fluctuations align with actual data findings, indicating that future measurements could potentially reveal the quark-gluon plasma's density distribution and distinguish between different models of the plasma's hadronization process.

We introduce a four-valued logic approach to enhance the consistency of query answers in databases. This framework includes an expanded version of four-valued logic that can handle databases with null values and identifies the relationships between consistency of query answers and four-valued logic evaluations. Next, we develop an algorithm to determine the consistency of query answers using four-valued logic evaluations and show that this algorithm has a polynomial time complexity for join queries. Finally, we compare our four-valued logic framework to existing methods that utilize three-valued logic in database consistency assessments.

This paper introduces the Time-Varying Poisson AutoRegressive with eXogenous covariates (TV-PARX) model, a dynamic extension of the PARX model, designed to capture the complex behavior of count time series under both exogenous influences and self-referential dynamics. We have reformulated the model using a continuous-time stochastic process and the Euler scheme to approximate its discrete-time form, enabling the application of various optimization methods for parameter estimation. The TV-PARX model effectively addresses nonlinear and time-varying components in data through the incorporation of polynomial functions and varying coefficients. Utilizing the functional form of the model, we can identify structural breaks by modeling segment-specific coefficients. The efficacy of the TV-PARX model is demonstrated through numerical examples and a real-world dataset analysis.

We introduce Neural Descriptor Networks, a novel framework that leverages Neural Descriptor Fields to define task-specific descriptors for end-to-end learning in robotics. This approach enables agents to successfully complete tasks through a single demonstration by learning a distribution over a set of natural language descriptors, rather than a vast action space. We demonstrate Neural Descriptor Networks' effectiveness in a real-world scenario by developing an automated system that, using only a few written instructions, can navigate a complex kitchen environment and execute a series of actions to find and pick up specific objects. This solution, which we call the "Kitchen Explorer," showcases the potential of Neural Descriptor Networks in a high-stakes application and highlights the benefits of its descriptor-based learning over traditional reinforcement learning methods.

Wilke constructed a three-dimensional N=2 and N=4 supersymmetric QCD model using a refined screening dimension of 1/2 and a $z$-factor of 1 for the fermion field, which, however, results in an inconsistent ghost system in the N=2 and an unacceptably large effective exponent in the N=4 scenario. In contrast, the Ito-Ishikawa model, introduced in 1996, offers alternative solutions for both the N=2 and N=4 supersymmetric QCD in three dimensions, utilizing a screening combination that includes multiple field transformations and yields a nonzero $z$-factor of 1.5 for the fermion field, thereby providing consistent ghost systems and more plausible effective exponents for both N=2 and N=4. In particular, the value of the complex scaling parameter $z_c$ increases from 0.75 to 1.5 when moving from N=2 to N=4.

We investigate the relationship between the performance of the approximate message passing algorithm for $ \Z_2$-synchronization and the TAP free energy at the algorithm's equilibrium point. Our analysis reveals that the algorithm's convergence is impeded by a spin-glass phase, which we define as the region where the TAP free energy takes a value less than its minimum within the set of all pure random ensembles. Our findings demonstrate that the algorithm's performance in the spin-glass phase matches its worst possible outcome in the most randomly generated ensemble, and that this performance can be either a lower bound or an upper bound, depending on whether the spin-glass phase is connected to the random ensemble phase or not. Our analysis also provides a criterion for determining the connectivity of the spin-glass phase, which is crucial for understanding the algorithm's performance in its spin-glass phase.

The reliance on nighttime photometry for determining vertical aerosol optical depth without absolute calibration is challenged by this work, which utilizes wide-field photometry during both day and night. A linear relationship between sky brightness and aerosol optical depth is supported by nighttime photometry, and by comparing the optical depths derived from nighttime and daytime observations, the study finds them to be equivalent with a small standard deviation. This equivalence is explained by the similar scattering of light by both daytime and nighttime atmospheric particles, and it is proposed that wide-field photometry during the day can serve as a calibration reference for vertical aerosol optical depth with minimal need for nighttime data. A note is also made on the limitations of this approach for narrow-field photometry, which is influenced more significantly by the field of view and is less robust to calibration errors.

Projecting groupings of 2D image features back into 3D space allows for the estimation of an object's pose. However, in complex, real-world scenes, multiple objects often overlap and project to the same 2D location, making it difficult to determine the appropriate projections to use for pose estimation. We present a method that addresses this challenge by introducing a novel projection selection metric and a strategy for automatically identifying and rejecting less reliable projections. Our approach, evaluated on the BOP Challenge dataset, outperforms the current state-of-the-art by a significant margin without the use of occlusion bounding boxes or the ground truth labels.

We introduce a new generalization of the Graphical Lasso model, called G-Lasso with latent variables, which extends the existing framework to accommodate hidden factors in multivariate Gaussian distributions. This model includes Graphical Lasso as a special case and enables the estimation of graphs representing both direct and indirect relationships between observable variables. Our generalization formulates an additional sparsity-inducing penalty on the off-diagonal elements of a matrix whose zeros correspond to non-existent latent connections, and we provide an algorithm for estimating these graphs using an augmented Graphical Lasso method. Our theoretical findings include both an $O(1/n)$-consistency result for estimating the underlying directed acyclic graph and an augmented Tikhonov matrix inverse, as well as an analysis of the group lasso with non-uniform weights. Our methodology and theoretical developments apply to both sparse and non-sparse G-Lasso with latent variables.

This study compares the performance of various numerical methods for different levels of model complexity in simulations of a prototypical biomolecular system, the alanine dipeptide. Evaluations were conducted using a range of numerical techniques, spanning traditional finite-difference methods to sophisticated deep learning-based approaches, including a proposed new deep learning method. Assessments were made of both computational efficiency and accuracy in reproducing the peptide's dynamics. Results across multiple levels of model complexity revealed that the most effective methods, despite varying depending on the level of modeling, consistently exhibited faster computation for similar accuracy when compared to the current standard. Notably, the deep learning-based methods, particularly the proposed one, demonstrated superior performance, surpassing the state-of-the-art Hamiltonian Neural Network and Exhibiting enhanced performance over the Hamiltonian Markov Chain Neural Network. A notable finding from this study is the introduction of a new performance metric, the model's ability to accurately capture the potential energy surface when applied to a longer timescale than typically simulated in biomolecular systems. This metric was utilized to evaluate the numerical methods and revealed that while highly efficient methods perform well in short timescales, there is a trade-off with less efficient methods offering better capture of the potential energy surface at longer timescales.

The concept of node importance has various applications in network analysis, but it is typically defined within a single layer and may yield inconsistent results when considering multiple layers. To address this limitation, we are investigating a type of inter-layer constraint that limits the comparison of node importance across different layers, such as enforcing consistency in ranking or setting a fixed ratio. These inter-layer constraints can be represented as a circular system of inequalities or a set of linear inequalities, and we develop an efficient method to calculate the spread of importance values in multilayer networks subject to these constraints. Our approach utilizes a modified version of the Kirchhoff model and computes the variance of importance distributions in multilayer networks. We then apply and evaluate our approach using synthetic and real-world multilayer networks, including a notable example from the field of gene co-expression networks.

We derive the Dirac equation in the $R$-Minkowski spacetime by starting from the Dirac equation in de Sitter spacetime and applying a suitable limit. The resulting equation matches the known formula in $R$-Minkowski spacetime obtained through other methods.

This study investigates the complex surface seal phenomenon occurring during a projectile's initial flight path, specifically at the base of a cylindrical cavity. To gain a deeper understanding of this process, a 2D axisymmetric surface seal model was developed and used to analyze high-speed impact data. Through computational simulations, pressure inside the cavity was examined in relation to different impact velocities. As the impact speed increased from 1.5 to 3.5 km/s, the pressure reduction within the cavity also rose, and its effects on surface seal dynamics were found to be significant. At higher impact speeds, the rear surface seal transforms into a complex process involving a rapid pressure decrease, followed by a brief period of surface separation, and finally, the sudden closure of the seal caused by the increased pressure inside the cavity. This behavior was validated through comparison with existing research and high-speed x-ray experiments.

We've developed a novel, generalized Witten effect that applies to gauge-gravity dualities. This generalized phenomenon replicates the original concept proposed by Witten, expanding on it to include various other effects stemming from the curl term in the gravity dual. By examining the curl term's impact on a scalar condensate within a specific background, we discovered it leads to a non-zero electric field in the associated dual theory. The resulting charged state spectrum can be reinterpreted as originating from a localised source in the dual theory. This discovery aligns with the concept of Witten effect, demonstrating that any charged state in the dual theory is equivalent to a localised source within the original background. The generalised Witten effect is particularly pertinent to the AdS soliton model, where it provides a more comprehensive understanding of the charged state spectrum, ultimately shedding light on the role of the curl term in the associated dual theory.

Cubanite, a rare mineral with a KTaO3 crystal structure, has been theoretically studied using first-principles methods to understand its unique electronic properties. By examining the band structure and density of states, we found that the material's charge stability and ferromagnetic ordering can be attributed to the interplay of filled oxygen bands and a single-electron degenerate d-orbital at the Fermi level, occurring due to the large lattice parameter. This result is supported by a calculation of the total energy as a function of internal pressure, which reveals that the charge stability is a direct consequence of the covalency between oxygen and cations. Additionally, we investigated the effects of different atomic positions and chemical substitutions on the electronic properties, including the effects of vacancies, which may be relevant to experimental findings.

Researchers who rely on laser driving forces to manipulate quantum systems are facing a significant challenge due to the variability of their experimental setup. A theoretical model suggests that even minor fluctuations in the driving frequency and power can lead to a loss of coherent interaction between a quantum dot and an acoustic cavity. This study experimentally verifies this prediction by demonstrating that controlled changes in the laser frequency can either bypass or disrupt the Rabi ratcheting phenomenon, even in a noisy environment. To achieve this, the authors manipulated the frequency and power of a laser beam to induce coherent interaction between a quantum dot and an acoustic cavity, and observed a transition from chaotic to periodic behavior in the photon output. This study highlights the importance of carefully calibrating the driving conditions to maintain the quantum coherence required for various applications.

We introduce a herringbone lattice model with tunable properties via the application of perturbations to its Hamiltonian. This model can be modified to emulate a variety of topological and semi-metallic scenarios, including the $J_1-J_2$ model, the Asymmetrical Dirac point, and the hexagonal warping, depending on the specific perturbations used. By modifying the herringbone lattice's geometry through the application of strain or by creating a superlattice, we successfully generate a herringbone lattice with a variety of structural parameters, including the lattice constant ratio, asymmetry in the sublattice dimensions, and the angle between the orientation of adjacent dimer bonds. By analyzing these parameters, we found that they can be manipulated to create a $J_1-J_2$ interaction, result in the folding of a hexagonal lattice, give rise to a cubic anisotropy in the energy dispersion, or even lead to the formation of a Dirac cone at the Fermi level. This versatility of the herringbone lattice makes it an attractive candidate for experimental realization and verification of predicted phenomena in materials science.

We developed single-photon catalyzed coherent states (SPCCSs) through two types of linear optical devices: beam splitters and parametric amplifiers. By analyzing various scenarios, our findings indicate that beam splitter generated SPCCSs exhibit significantly higher success probabilities for a certain input photon number, whereas the probabilities associated with parametric amplifiers are generally much lower. Our research demonstrates that SPCCCSs can be created using beam splitters with arbitrary reflectivities, offering the potential for using readily available optical components to generate SPCCCSs and thereby increase the effectiveness of quantum Catalytic Catalysis.

The Newman-Penrose formalism's complex coefficients of the Weyl tensor in the $(2,2)$-type are expressed in the Newman-Penrose equations' complex conjugate forms. This is demonstrated by applying the complex conjugate operation to the original equations, taking the specific example of a Schwarzschild black hole's Weyl tensor. This results in a set of complex conjugate equations that can be solved for the complex coefficients of the $(2,2)$-type, allowing the recovery of the original equations through complex conjugation.

A new statistical framework is introduced to represent complex objects, such as polymers, using their individual components. This method, based on a mixture of Dirac delta functions in a general space, allows for the inference of unknown objects using only observed, related data. A non-parametric Bayesian approach is then used to perform this object inference, resulting in a Bayesian non-parametric delta process in the general space. This technique was specifically developed to represent and infer the configuration of a polymer based on its end-to-end distance measurements. The associated algorithm can effectively handle multiple measurements and provide a distribution of probable polymer configurations. This method is demonstrated through applications in both simulated and real data sets.

This study proposes a novel attention-based unet model, known as Dilated Dense Attention Unet, and applies it to automatically identify and outline tumors in esophageal scans. Medical imaging segmentation challenges are addressed by the proposed method, which uses co-occurrence networks to implement both a Dilated Dense Attention module and a spatial attention component, effectively directing the network's focus towards critical anatomical features while simplifying the classification task to a binary decision between healthy and diseased tissue. The experimental results show that the Dilated Dense Attention Unet achieves superior performance in esophageal tumor segmentation compared to other advanced models, including the original unet.

The rise of multilingual societies necessitates high-quality, multilingual NLP systems, and our work contributes to this requirement by developing a unified framework for multilingual NLP pretraining, which enhances performance and expands to new languages without further training. Leveraging a massive multilingual corpus without explicit separation, our model employs a shared wordpiece layer and a unified transformer-based encoder, and we introduce a ranking-based sentence selection strategy to improve data efficiency and representation diversity. Our framework achieves outstanding results in multiple tasks and sets new benchmarks for several languages and language pairs in WMT evaluations. Specifically, it attains scores of 43.36 in automatic evaluation for the Czech news translation task and 41.18 in automatic evaluation for the Bulgarian news translation task. Additionally, our framework excels in other evaluations and zero-shot and few-shot subtasks within the WMT evaluation platform.

The rise of visually impaired users on social media platforms like Instagram highlights the need for a better image description generation model, one that can effectively capture both visual and metadata information. To address this challenge, we present a multi-task convolutional neural network model, capable of simultaneously performing image classification, object detection, and text-based description generation. The model's design minimizes task isolation, enabling the exchange of rich intermediate data between tasks and enhancing performance through a shared learned representation. Evaluating the model on both visual classification and image description generation tasks shows significant performance improvements over baseline models. The code for this research is available on GitHub at https://github.com/zhongrudong/CMT.

To accurately model energy loss functions for tantalum oxide layers, particularly in vacuum tantalum oxide tantalum double layers, theoretical calculations must account for both local field effects and chemical shifts or shifts due to spin-orbit coupling. When these effects are considered, in the energy loss function around the Fermi level, a local minimum appears near 2 eV and a peak emerges near 3 eV. These features align with experimental findings obtained through angle-resolved photoemission and spectroscopy, suggesting that a comprehensive understanding of these energy loss functions relies on multi-band and effective models of tantalum and oxide layers, incorporating local field effects, chemical shifts, and spin-orbit coupling through a simplified but realistic approach.

The increasing separation of people into distinct social groups based on shared characteristics, a phenomenon observed by social critic Bill McKibben as 'The Big Sort', has been linked to the spread of misinformation. According to this theory, as individuals move to areas with people who share their same views and values, their social connections become more insulated from opposing perspectives and critical fact-checking, making it easier for them to accept and disseminate false information. This study investigates the impact of geographic segregation on the online spread of misinformation by examining the behavior of users in real-world online communities. We analyzed a large dataset of 18 million online posts from the Reddit platform and employed a computational model to simulate the spread of misinformation within these communities. Our findings suggest that geographic segregation accelerates the online spread of misinformation in both rural and urban areas. In areas with significant geographic segregation, misinformation can spread to a larger number of users and becomes more resistant to being debunked. We also discovered that the influence of geographic segregation on the spread of misinformation is more pronounced when the communities in question are more socially connected.

This study investigates the underlying factors that influence the semantic structure of speech used in teaching, with a focus on identifying the relationships between speech and visual demonstrations. We analyzed a large dataset of instruction-giving tasks, encompassing both demonstrations with and without audio components. Our findings reveal that the semantic structure of speech is shaped by multiple variables, including the type of demonstration, whether audio instructions are provided, the presence of subtasks, and errors made during the demonstration. We also developed a computational method to automatically generate corresponding text based on visual demonstrations, and utilized both human evaluations and automatic metrics to assess the semantic similarity between the generated text and the actual speech. Our research demonstrates improvements in both the quality of the speech and the semantic similarity when using a combination of both audio and visual components of the demonstrations, and also shows that the most effective type of instruction varies depending on the task.

In 1997, Witten introduced a classical field theory model, which led to a deeper understanding of the relationship between Yang-Mills fields and the geometry of a manifold. Building on this work, he derived the Euler-Arnold equations and demonstrated their connection to Yang-Mills fields in the presence of specific boundary conditions. Subsequent research revealed that these equations represent an optimal solution to a variational problem arising from quantum field theory, specifically in the context of topological sigma models. The current study generalizes the Euler-Arnold equations to a level 1 Nambu-Goto string theory, resulting in a modified geodesic equation that defines a new Euler-Arnold flow. This transformation is shown to transform the Euler-Arnold equations into a set of coupled Euler-Arnold equations, leading to an in-depth analysis of the variational problem and its connection to the geodesic flow. The study also explores the topological invariants associated with the Euler-Arnold equations and presents explicit examples of Euler-Arnold flows on a sphere and a torus.

Conversational systems rely on sophisticated testing frameworks to ensure functionality and accuracy. However, testing these systems has become increasingly difficult due to their dynamic nature. Many existing automated testing frameworks for conversational systems fall short because of poorly defined test data generation methods, limited scalability, and inadequate support for complex system testing. In response to these limitations, we present a novel end-to-end automated testing framework for conversational systems, leveraging reinforcement learning to enhance effectiveness and efficiency. The framework includes a central component that manages multiple automated testers, leveraging a custom designed protocol to ensure seamless performance. To facilitate wide adoption, we open-source the framework, along with a sample implementation utilizing Python and TensorFlow, and provide guidance on customization and integration. Notably, we demonstrate the framework's capabilities by successfully testing a real-world application, showcasing its versatility and adaptability.

To address the challenge of dynamic user preferences in recommendation systems, a new approach called Gated Aspect Preference Enhancement (GAPE) has been developed. GAPE introduces a module that selectively updates user preferences based on the relevance of specific item aspects, successfully improving the performance of the system. Theoretical analysis of the stability and convergence of the system's dynamics was then conducted, revealing that the GAPE model achieves both improved stability and a higher convergence rate than a comparable baseline. The effectiveness of GAPE was further validated through experiments conducted on multiple real-world datasets, demonstrating its superior performance over alternative models.

To analyze and compare natural formulations using exotic cones and extended formulations for various optimization problems, including flow, cut, and traveling salesman variations, a new framework is introduced. This framework provides dimensions and specific structural characteristics for both exotic and extended formulations, enabling an examination of the dimensionality and complexity of both approaches. Through this examination, both the dimensions of the formulations and the difficulty of deriving them are found to be similar for both exotic and extended formulations, demonstrating that both methods are essentially equivalent and that the term "exotic formulation" is misleading. Consequently, the term should be replaced with "equivalent formulation".

A significant challenge in developing MRI analysis models lies in their limited generalizability, which can be attributed to the diverse range of acquisition protocols and imaging parameters used in clinical settings. This study investigates the impact of a heterogeneous dataset on model performance through a novel task called MRI style transfer, where the aim is to modify the appearance of an MRI by combining two distinct styles, represented by two different datasets. We introduce a quantitative measure called the performance separation score to evaluate the effectiveness of this transfer in improving model accuracy on an unseen dataset. We further explore the potential benefits of style transfer in homogeneous transfer, where the goal is to improve model performance on a specific protocol or sequence type, such as transferring from multi-contrast to single-contrast scans. Through a novel multi-style adversarial network, we demonstrate the feasibility of style transfer in both homogeneous and heterogeneous transfer scenarios. The study concludes by examining the limitations of current techniques and identifying areas for future research in this field.

This work introduces a comprehensive network-based multi-agent optimization framework, which categorizes problems into 3 categories and provides a general algorithm for solving a representative case study.

The Motivation Dynamics model, initially developed for single-agent scenarios, has been expanded to accommodate multiple agents. This expansion maintains the same descriptive simplicity as the original model. The multi-agent version of Motivation Dynamics effectively captures various strategic interactions, including a pivotal rendezvous behavior, which the single-agent model cannot replicate. By incorporating the multi-agent Motivation Dynamics model and leveraging its modular structure, we gain insight into rendezvous behavior through the lens of a specific parameter, referred to as the rendezvous factor. This factor, which arises naturally from the model, can be used to analyze the properties of rendezvous behaviors in multiple-agent systems.

Our research investigated the electronic and crystallographic properties of GdxCm(1-x)Sn3 compounds, specifically focusing on the composition range where Gd and Cm coexist. We analyzed the results of specific heat, magnetization, and powder x-ray diffraction studies on Gd1.2Cm0.8Sn3, Gd0.8Cm1.2Sn3, Gd0.7Cm1.3Sn3, and Gd0.6Cm1.4Sn3 compounds. The x-ray diffraction data confirmed that all compounds have the same AuCu3 crystal structure. The specific heat measurements revealed an increase in the magnetic moment of GdxCm(1-x)Sn3 as Cm composition increases, from 7.7 μB per atom for Gd1.2Cm0.8Sn3 to 8.1 μB per atom for Gd0.8Cm1.2Sn3, Gd0.7Cm1.3Sn3, and finally 8.5 μB per atom for Gd0.6Cm1.4Sn3. The enhanced magnetic moment in Gd0.6Cm1.4Sn3 is attributed to the 7s electrons of Cm contributing to the magnetic moment, as predicted by an ab initio calculation.

Our study focuses on the interaction of charmed and bottom quarks within the framework of QCD, seeking to accurately describe how these quarks interact via a charm-bottom quark pair. To achieve this, we employ a computational method that enables the evaluation of complex integrals and apply it to calculate the charm-bottom quark interaction in a state of polarization, specifically in the $B_s$ system. By leveraging this calculation, we can determine the difference in masses between the heavy quarks and refine the prediction for the mass difference between the $B^0$ and $\bar{B}^0$ states.

This research investigates the properties of a modified standard Coxeter group known as the finite classical Coxeter group Bn under its symmetric group representation, denoted as sgn. The exchange law for the generalized standard basis of Bn is examined in relation to its Coxeter length and descent set. The study reveals that applying any braid operation resulting from a generator or the inverse of a generator to the set of Bn's minimal elements will yield a subset of the set of minimal elements that has the same cardinality. Furthermore, the study demonstrates that applying any braid operation to the set of Bn's maximal elements will yield the set of maximal elements itself. The research also explores the connection between the exchange law for the generalized standard basis of Bn and its Coxeter length, revealing that it corresponds to the number of simple reflections involved in a specific sequence of operations, known as the Coxeter cycle.

The project aims to create an open database of halo properties for various types of galaxies based on observations and simulations. The database currently includes 4500 observed galaxies and 20000 simulated galaxies, with their halos analyzed using three different methods. Limiting the study to galaxies with total masses between $10^{9.5}$ and $10^{11.5} \, \text{M}_\odot$, the researchers compared the distribution of subhalos, substructure, and satellite galaxies in the cores of their parent halos. The study of subhalos revealed that their maximum circular velocities are directly proportional to the square root of the host halo's mass, indicating a fundamental relationship that constrains the halos' assembly processes. Furthermore, the study found that subhalos with specific masses become stable, with the peak of their mass function shifting from $10^{7.5}$ to $10^{9.5} \, \text{M}_\odot$ as the host halo's mass increases from $10^{9.5}$ to $10^{11.5} \, \text{M}_\odot$. The researchers also discovered that the distribution of subhalos within the core of a galaxy halo is well-explained by a power-law model with an index of $-3.5$, indicating that smaller subhalos are more densely packed towards the center. The study of a specific type of defect in diamond known as T centres has been ongoing for nearly a century. Despite their intriguing optical and quantum properties, T centres have not been widely utilized in quantum technologies due to the lack of understanding of their behavior in multi-photon interactions. This research investigated T centres embedded in nanoscale diamond cavities using a sophisticated spectroscopic technique that revealed a complex diffusion pattern in their optical spectra. The findings suggest that T centres tend to cluster together, implying that their optical properties are influenced by both the local environment and the interaction with the surrounding defects. The analysis revealed that the T centres' ability to engage in multi-photon interactions could lead to the creation of rare quantum entanglements, and that increasing the number of T centres enhances this phenomenon. The study also demonstrated that the distribution of T centres can be manipulated to optimize their quantum properties for specific applications. The research paves the way for further investigation into the quantum properties of T centres in diamond cavities, offering a promising foundation for developing quantum devices that utilize these defects.

Deep neural network-based object detectors have shown superior performance in various
tasks, and the choice among them often hinges on the specific application at hand.
In an attempt to create a general purpose object detector that adapts to different
settings, we propose a novel way to modify the target of the object detection task.
The approach involves training a single object detector that can adapt to a particular
distribution of environments, without requiring multiple models for each setting.
We achieve this by introducing a distribution-aware loss function that incorporates
uncertainty about the underlying distribution of environments, and we employ a prior
over the set of object detection models as a way to condition the detector on a given
environment. The proposed method is demonstrated to be effective in adapting to new
settings when compared to alternative solutions, and we provide guidelines for choosing
hyperparameters based on a simple grid search. The approach is shown to be broadly
applicable, including both pre-trained detectors on a large dataset like ImageNet, and
hand-designed detectors for specific applications.

This article examines the existence and uniqueness of solutions to a system of elliptic partial differential equations, considering various types of function behaviors. Our primary focus is on a recent uniqueness result by Gagnidze and Gurtun, which requires the decay of a specific function, $f_i$, to be no larger than $x^{-2}$ for some solutions to the Dirichlet problem for the Laplace equation in $\mathbb{R}^2$. We demonstrate that this condition is overly restrictive by providing a unique solution to the Dirichlet problem for the Laplace equation in $\mathbb{R}^2$, even when one of the input functions, $f_i$, decays at the rate $x^{-1}$. We also investigate other scenarios, including the Dirichlet problem for the biharmonic equation in $\mathbb{R}^2$ and a boundary value problem for a certain elliptic system of differential equations in $\mathbb{R}^n$.

Conditioning independent Bernoulli random variables on their sum yields a system of dependent and identically distributed random variables. This dependency reduces over time, and we can derive various inequalities to analyze it. Initially, we show that the hyperbolicity of the system through time $n$ is equivalent to a specific $1/2$-norm bounded by a constant, which enables us to prove a concentration inequality for convex functions with a simplified approach. This can also be applied to obtain an almost sure convergence result for a specific class of polynomial functions. Furthermore, we establish an independent result demonstrating that conditioning independent random variables typically leads to a decline in variance, which we measure as a specific hyperbolicity property.

For the symplectic group $Sp_4(K)$ over a field $K$, we categorize the conjugacy classes using a system of invariants consisting of a non-degenerate quadratic form $\delta$ in two variables and a non-trivial element $\sigma$ from the group $\Gamma_2(K)$.

The incompatibility between potential donors and recipients poses a significant challenge in kidney transplantation. A new model has been developed that treats incompatibility as a dynamic state within a Markov Decision Process framework, enabling the exploration of strategies for matching donors and recipients. By incorporating incompatibility as a state variable, the model reveals the value of replacing the current incompatibility state through a learning process. The model's properties were examined under both perfect and imperfect knowledge of incompatibility states. In the case of perfect knowledge, the model's optimal policy simplifies to prioritizing the most incompatible match over time. The analysis also highlights the benefits of recruiting new donors in response to changing preferences of registered recipients. The model's theoretical findings are further validated through a numerical study using real-world data. The associated software code is available for public use.

This paper undertakes an examination of word relationships in financial text-based embeddings, specifically focusing on the representation of antonyms in models like EML and ERNIE-TS. We highlight the shortcomings of current embedding techniques, which incorrectly treat antonyms as "frequentist synonyms" by learning representations that indicate both terms are likely to occur frequently in the same context. We argue this issue is particularly problematic in financial contexts due to the differing frequencies of opposing terms, such as "profit" and "loss." To address this problem, this study proposes a novel task-specific approach called the Contrastive Similarity Learning model, which employs a contrastive learning framework to capture the true semantic relationships of antonyms in financial text-based embeddings. Experimental results using the FIANEL dataset demonstrate that our model excels over the EML and ERNIE-TS models in accurately capturing antonymous relationships, as evaluated by the Antonym Relation Embedding Task.

In wideband waveforming applications, allocating time slots or frequencies is crucial. A common goal is to minimize the maximum throughput among all users while ensuring fair throughput for each user. However, determining optimal solutions for these fair-throughput and sum-throughput optimization problems is challenging due to their non-linear and non-convex nature. This study develops efficient algorithms to solve these problems. Specifically, a gradient-based method is proposed to maximize fair throughput and a dual-decomposition algorithm is developed to optimize sum throughput. Both algorithms leverage partial user data and can be executed in a distributed manner. Theoretical performance guarantees are established for the fair-throughput optimization algorithm. Numerical experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed algorithms and provide insights into their performance in various scenarios.

This study introduces a mathematical framework to replicate the Rayleigh–Bénard instability found in fluids by leveraging a multiscale approach combining a low-resolution fluid model and a high-resolution plate model. To mitigate computational inefficiencies, we employ a novel boundary control method that applies a targeted, brief disturbance to the plate to replicate the desired instability patterns. This approach overcomes difficulties associated with modeling short-scale, three-dimensional instability patterns near the plate and enables us to effectively capture the Rayleigh–Bénard instability through a controlled boundary condition. By applying this technique in a multiscale simulation, we successfully replicate the characteristics of the Rayleigh–Bénard instability in a single-domain setting, even in a narrow domain with a large aspect ratio.

We present an innovative reinforcement learning framework called the Iterative Elimination Agent, which guides players towards bypassing iteratively dominated actions in dynamic settings. The agent's underlying mechanism involves a systematic elimination process based on counterfactual learning, ensuring that players can identify and steer clear of previous mistakes. We demonstrate theoretical convergence of our approach, showing that in time, the average payoff obtained by the learner will asymptotically approach the maximum possible payoff in a given environment. Additionally, we provide a practical algorithm incorporating a sample efficiency exploration strategy and validate our method through successful applications in both simulated and real-world game scenarios.

Network dynamics have been extensively used to model various phenomena, including the spread of epidemics, where node connections represent interactions between individuals and influence the epidemic's progression. Recent studies indicate that the long-term outcomes of these networks are often random and take on either all-or-nothing patterns. To investigate this further, we developed a stochastic model where network rewiring leads to random outcomes, and our analysis revealed a key finding: the model can exhibit all-or-nothing patterns even when the network is completely randomized. We further found that introducing random variability can lead to a significant decrease in the fraction of infected individuals, with this decrease becoming more pronounced as the network's connectivity increases. We also explored a generalized version of the model where node connections can vary in strength, and our results showed that the all-or-nothing pattern persists even in this more complex scenario.

A key aspect of fitting parton distribution functions (PDFs) is accounting for the DGLAP evolution, which describes how PDFs change across different energy scales. In a fit to available data, the DGLAP evolution can be incorporated into a global fit using an integral equation, which ensures consistency across the range of energy scales studied. This approach is particularly important when analyzing deep-inelastic scattering (DIS) data at various scales, as it enables the extraction of general PDF parameters that can be applied across different energy scales. In the context of the NNPDF fit methodology, the DGLAP evolution is incorporated into a series of integral equations that match the renormalization group invariance of PDFs. This is achieved by solving a set of nonlinear integral equations, which are derived from the convolution term in the PDF generator, and include contributions from the DGLAP evolution, non-perturbative effects, and external data. By solving these integral equations, the PDFs can be determined at any desired energy scale, and this approach has been successfully applied to fits of DIS data at NLO and NNLO in QCD. However, when extending this approach to fits of modern PDFs, which include larger datasets (e.g. jet production in $e^+e^-$ collisions, semi-inclusive deep-inelastic scattering, and hadron collider data), the DGLAP evolution becomes more complex and cannot be captured by a set of integral equations.
